title: Feedback & Real Op Amps
description: Negative feedback in numbers, and what real op amps do to it: offsets, bias currents, bandwidth, slew rate, stability and comparators.

study.title: The golden rules and when they fail
study.body: With negative feedback and the op amp in its linear range: **(I)** the output does whatever is needed to make the voltage difference between the inputs zero; **(II)** the inputs draw no current. Rule I fails when the loop cannot do its job: output clipped at a rail, output slewing, signal frequency near the bandwidth limit, inputs outside the common-mode range, or no (or positive) feedback as in comparators. Rule II is only approximate: real inputs draw a bias current $I_B$ (pA for FET inputs, nA for BJT inputs).

study.title: The feedback equation
study.body: A fraction $B$ of the output is subtracted from the input of an amplifier with open-loop gain $A$. The **loop gain** $AB$ is the gain 'left over'; when $AB \gg 1$ the closed-loop gain is $1/B$, set by the resistors (noninverting amp: $1/B = 1 + R_2/R_1$). Changes in $A$ are reduced by $1+AB$: $dG/G = (dA/A)/(1+AB)$. Feedback in series with the input raises $Z_{in}$ by $1+AB$; feedback sampling the output voltage lowers $Z_{out}$ by $1+AB$.

study.title: Offset voltage and bias current
study.body: Model the offset $V_{os}$ as a small battery in series with the + input: it is amplified by the **noise gain** $1 + R_2/R_1$, also in an inverting amplifier. Bias current into the − input flows through $R_2$ and adds $I_BR_2$. A resistor $R_3 = R_1 \parallel R_2$ in series with the + input cancels the bias-current part, leaving only $I_{os}R_2$ (offset current $I_{os}$ is typically $I_B$/2 to $I_B$/10).

study.title: Explore: gain–bandwidth product
study.body: An internally compensated op amp rolls off at 6 dB/octave (20 dB/decade) from a few Hz, reaching unity gain at $f_T$ (here 1 MHz). With feedback the closed-loop gain follows the open-loop curve once $A$ drops to the noise gain $G$, so the bandwidth is $f_T/G$. The large-signal limit is the **slew rate** SR: a sine of peak $V_p$ needs $2\pi f V_p \le$ SR, so full power is available only up to $f_{max} = SR/(2\pi V_p)$.

study.title: Explore: compensation and phase margin
study.body: The dominant pole gives 90° lag and a second pole $f_2$ adds more; at 180° lag with loop gain ≥ 1 the amplifier oscillates. **Phase margin** is 180° minus the lag at the crossover $f_c$ where $|AB| = 1$ (aim for ≥ 45°). Unity-gain-stable op amps put $f_T$ below $f_2$ for the worst case $B = 1$, which makes them slow; decompensated types are faster but need a minimum noise gain. A capacitive load adds a pole with the output resistance: use a small series resistor. Graph: $f_T$ = 50 MHz, $f_2$ = 10 MHz.

study.title: Output limits and single-supply operation
study.body: A classic op amp output swings to within 1–2 V of each rail and delivers about 20 mA; **rail-to-rail** types get within tens of mV, and some inputs also work down to (or beyond) the rails. On a single supply, bias the signal at $V_{CC}/2$: a divider $R_A = R_B$ sets the + input, $C_1$ couples the signal in, and $C_2$ makes the dc gain 1 so the output also sits at $V_{CC}/2$. The ac gain is $1 + R_2/R_1$.

study.title: Comparators and Schmitt triggers
study.body: A comparator is built for open-loop use: fast, no compensation, quick recovery, often an open-collector output with a pull-up. An op amp used this way is slow. **Positive feedback** gives hysteresis: the threshold depends on the output state, so a slow, noisy input causes one clean transition. In the inverting Schmitt trigger drawn (output $\pm V_{sat}$) the thresholds are $\pm V_{sat}R_1/(R_1+R_2)$:

steps.title: The golden rules
steps.body:
Horowitz & Hill's two rules for op amps with negative feedback:
- **I.** The output does whatever is needed to make $v_+ - v_- = 0$.
- **II.** The inputs draw no current.
Rule I is a consequence of feedback with huge gain, so it only holds while the op amp *can* respond: not clipped, not slewing, within its bandwidth and common-mode range.

steps.prompt: In which case can you still use golden rule I ($v_+ = v_-$)?
options: A ×10 amplifier at 1 kHz whose output stays 3 V from either rail
An amplifier whose output is clipped at the positive rail
A Schmitt trigger (feedback to the + input)
steps.explanation: Rule I needs working negative feedback. A clipped output can no longer move to correct the input difference, a comparator has no feedback, and a Schmitt trigger has positive feedback, so its inputs differ on purpose. The ×10 amplifier at 1 kHz is well inside its linear range.

steps.title: The feedback equation
steps.body: The amplifier sees $v_{in} - Bv_{out}$, so $v_{out} = A(v_{in} - Bv_{out})$. Solving gives the closed-loop gain below. The product $AB$ is the **loop gain**: the gain around the loop. If $AB \gg 1$, $G \approx 1/B$: the gain depends only on the feedback network, not on the op amp.

steps.prompt: An amplifier with open-loop gain $A$ = {{A}} gets feedback with $B$ = 1/{{G0}}.

ask.prompt: Find the loop gain $AB$.
Find the closed-loop gain.
ask.explanation: $G = \frac{A}{1+AB}$ = {{A}} / (1 + {{A/G0}}) = {{A/(1+A/G0)||4}}, a little below the ideal $1/B$ = {{G0}}.

ask.prompt: By what percentage is the gain below the ideal value $1/B$?
ask.explanation: The relative error is $\frac{1}{1+AB}$ = 1/(1 + {{A/G0}}) = {{100/(1+A/G0)}} %. More loop gain, less error.

steps.prompt: An op amp's open-loop gain $A$ = {{A}} drops by {{dA}} % when it warms up. It is used in a noninverting amplifier with $B$ = 1/{{G0}}. By how many percent does the closed-loop gain **drop**? For a change this large, use the loop gain **after** the change.
steps.hint: $\Delta G/G = (\Delta A/A)/(1+AB)$, with $AB$ computed from the new $A$.
steps.explanation:
Feedback divides the change by $1+AB$. For a large change use the loop gain with the **new** $A$ = {{A*(1-dA/100)}}: $AB$ = {{A*(1-dA/100)/G0}}.
$\frac{\Delta G}{G} = \frac{\Delta A/A}{1+AB}$ = {{dA}} % / {{1+A*(1-dA/100)/G0}} = {{dA/(1 + A*(1 - dA/100)/G0)}} %. (This is exact: $G_1 - G_2 = \frac{A_1-A_2}{(1+A_1B)(1+A_2B)}$.)

steps.title: Feedback changes impedances
steps.body: In a noninverting amplifier the feedback voltage is in **series** with the input: the input only has to supply the tiny error voltage, so $Z_{in}$ rises by $1+AB$. Because feedback senses the output voltage, $Z_{out}$ drops by $1+AB$. In an inverting amplifier the feedback is in **shunt** at the input: the − input is a virtual ground and $Z_{in} = R_1$.

steps.prompt: A BJT-input op amp has $A$ = {{A}}, open-loop input resistance $Z_i$ = {{Zi|Ω}} and output resistance $Z_o$ = {{Zo|Ω}}. It is used as a noninverting amplifier with gain {{G0}}.

ask.prompt: Find the input impedance.
ask.explanation:
$B = 1/G$, so $AB$ = {{A}}/{{G0}} = {{A/G0}}.
$Z_{in} = Z_i(1+AB)$ = {{Zi|Ω}} × {{1+A/G0}} = {{Zi*(1+A/G0)|Ω}}. (In practice the common-mode input resistance and leakage limit this.)

ask.prompt: Find the output impedance.
ask.explanation: $AB$ = {{A/G0}}, so $Z_{out} = \frac{Z_o}{1+AB}$ = {{Zo|Ω}} / {{1+A/G0}} = {{Zo/(1+A/G0)|Ω}}. It rises at high frequency, where $A$ falls.

steps.prompt: Negative feedback raises the input impedance of an inverting amplifier far above $R_1$.
steps.explanation: In the inverting amplifier the feedback holds the − input at virtual ground, so the source sees just $R_1$ to ground: $Z_{in} = R_1$. The $(1+AB)$ boost applies to series feedback at the input, as in the noninverting amplifier.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Gain of the op amp alone
Part of the output fed back
Excess gain that makes rule I work
Gain applied to errors at the input
steps.explanation: $A$ is huge and poorly defined; $B$ is set by the resistors. Their product, the loop gain, determines how accurate, stable and low-impedance the circuit is. The noise gain $1/B = 1 + R_2/R_1$ multiplies input-referred errors such as $V_{os}$, even in an inverting amplifier.

lessons.title: DC errors: offset and bias current

steps.prompt: The input of an inverting amplifier is grounded. The op amp is ideal except for its offset, modelled as $V_{os}$ = {{Vos|V}} in series with the + input.

ask.prompt: Find the output voltage.
ask.explanation:
Rule I puts the − input at $V_{os}$, so $R_1$ carries $V_{os}/R_1$, which also flows through $R_2$:
$v_o = V_{os}\left(1+\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)$ = {{Vos|V}} × {{1+R2/R1}} = {{V_U1|V}}.

ask.prompt: By what factor is $V_{os}$ amplified?
ask.explanation: The offset sees the **noise gain** $1 + R_2/R_1$ = {{1+R2/R1}}, not the signal gain $R_2/R_1$ = {{R2/R1}}: the output is {{V_U1|V}}.

steps.prompt: The input is grounded and the + input is tied to ground. The op amp draws a bias current $I_B$ = {{IB|A}} into its − input (modelled as a current source). Find the output voltage.
steps.explanation:
The − input sits at 0 V (rule I), so $R_1$ carries no current. All of $I_B$ must come from the output through $R_2$:
$v_o = I_BR_2$ = {{IB|A}} × {{R2|Ω}} = {{V_U1|V}}.

steps.prompt: An inverting amplifier has $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. The op amp has $I_B$ = {{IB|A}} and $I_{os}$ = {{Ios|A}}.

ask.prompt: Without $R_3$ (+ input grounded), estimate the output error due to $I_B$.
Which $R_3$ cancels the bias-current error?
ask.explanation: $R_3 = R_1 \parallel R_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}: both inputs then see the same resistance, so equal bias currents give equal voltage drops.

ask.prompt: With $R_3 = R_1 \parallel R_2$, estimate the remaining output error.
ask.explanation: Only the difference between the two input currents remains: $v_o \approx I_{os}R_2$ = {{Ios|A}} × {{R2|Ω}} = {{Ios*R2|V}}, against {{IB*R2|V}} without $R_3$.

steps.prompt: A noninverting amplifier with gain {{G}} uses $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} (no bias compensation). The op amp has $V_{os}$ = {{Vos|V}} and $I_B$ = {{IB|A}}. Estimate the worst-case output error with the input at 0 V.
steps.explanation:
Offset: $V_{os}(1 + R_2/R_1)$ = {{Vos|V}} × {{G}} = {{Vos*G|V}}.
Bias current: $I_BR_2$ = {{IB|A}} × {{R2|Ω}} = {{IB*R2|V}}.
Worst case they add: {{Vos*G + IB*R2|V}}.

steps.prompt: The offset of a ×{{G}} amplifier is trimmed to zero at 25 °C. The op amp's offset drift is {{TC*1e6}} µV/°C. How much does the output drift if the temperature rises {{dT}} °C?
steps.explanation: $\Delta V_{os}$ = {{TC*1e6}} µV/°C × {{dT}} °C = {{TC*dT|V}}; times the noise gain {{G}}: {{TC*dT*G|V}}. Trimming removes the initial offset, not the drift: precision work needs a low-drift op amp.

steps.prompt: In an inverting amplifier with gain −10, an input offset voltage $V_{os}$ produces an output offset of $10V_{os}$.
steps.explanation: The offset sits in series with the + input and sees the noise gain $1 + R_2/R_1$ = 11, so the output offset is $11V_{os}$. The signal gain (−10) and the noise gain differ.

steps.prompt: A photodiode amplifier uses a 10 MΩ feedback resistor. Which op amp gives the smallest dc output error?
steps.explanation: With 10 MΩ the bias current dominates: 100 nA × 10 MΩ = 1 V and 20 nA × 10 MΩ = 0.2 V, while 10 pA × 10 MΩ = 0.1 mV. The FET op amp's 1 mV offset (noise gain ≈ 1 here) is small by comparison. Rule of thumb: high resistances call for FET inputs.

steps.prompt: Match each dc-error problem to a good cure.
pairs: Trim it, or choose a precision op amp
Add $R_1 \parallel R_2$ in series with the + input
steps.explanation: Trimming fixes the initial offset but not its drift. Bias compensation cancels equal input currents, leaving $I_{os}R_2$. FET inputs have pA bias currents. A capacitor in series with $R_1$ of a noninverting amplifier reduces the dc noise gain to 1, so the offset is not amplified.

steps.prompt: An op amp has $f_T$ = {{fT|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the bandwidth of a noninverting amplifier with gain +{{G}}.
ask.explanation: Noise gain = signal gain = {{G}}: $f_{-3dB} \approx f_T/G$ = {{fT|Hz}} / {{G}} = {{fT/G|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the bandwidth of an inverting amplifier with gain −{{G}}.
ask.explanation:
The bandwidth is set by the **noise gain** $1 + R_2/R_1$ = {{G+1}}, not by $R_2/R_1$:
$f_{-3dB} \approx$ {{fT|Hz}} / {{G+1}} = {{fT/(G+1)|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: You need a gain of 100 with at least 50 kHz bandwidth, using op amps with $f_T$ = 1 MHz. Which works?
steps.explanation: One ×100 stage only reaches 1 MHz/100 = 10 kHz, whatever the resistor values. Each ×10 stage has 100 kHz bandwidth; two identical poles in cascade give about 0.64 × 100 kHz ≈ 64 kHz overall. Splitting gain over stages buys bandwidth.

steps.prompt: An op amp has a slew rate of {{SR/1e6}} V/µs.

ask.prompt: Up to what frequency can it deliver an undistorted sine of {{Vp|V}} peak?
ask.explanation:
A sine $V_p\sin(2\pi ft)$ has maximum slope $2\pi fV_p$. Set it equal to SR:
$f_{max} = \frac{SR}{2\pi V_p}$ = {{SR/1e6}} × 10⁶ V/s / (2π × {{Vp|V}}) = {{SR/(2*pi*Vp)|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: What is the largest undistorted peak amplitude at {{f|Hz}}?
ask.explanation: $V_p = \frac{SR}{2\pi f}$ = {{SR/1e6}} × 10⁶ V/s / (2π × {{f|Hz}}) = {{SR/(2*pi*f)|V}}. Larger signals turn into triangles.

steps.prompt: Op amp with $f_T$ = 1 MHz. Set the noise gain so the closed-loop bandwidth is {{fb|Hz}} (dashed line).
steps.explanation: $f_{-3dB} \approx f_T/G$, so $G = f_T/f_{-3dB}$ = 1 MHz / {{fb|Hz}} = {{Gt}} ({{20*log10(Gt)|dB}}). The flat closed-loop line meets the falling open-loop line exactly there.

steps.prompt: An amplifier with gain {{G}} must deliver an undistorted {{Vp|V}} peak sine at frequencies up to {{f|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the minimum slew rate in V/µs.
ask.explanation: SR ≥ $2\pi fV_p$ = 2π × {{f|Hz}} × {{Vp|V}} = {{2*pi*f*Vp/1e6}} V/µs. Choose a part with some margin.

ask.prompt: Find the minimum $f_T$ so that {{f|Hz}} is still within the −3 dB bandwidth.
ask.explanation: $f_T \ge G \cdot f$ = {{G}} × {{f|Hz}} = {{G*f|Hz}}. For a gain error well below 3 dB at that frequency, take 5–10 times more.

steps.prompt: An op amp has $f_T$ = {{fT|Hz}} and a second pole at $f_2$ = {{f2|Hz}}. It is used with noise gain {{G}}. Estimate the phase margin, taking the crossover at $f_c \approx f_T/G$.
steps.explanation:
$f_c \approx f_T/G$ = {{fT/G|Hz}}. The dominant pole gives 90° lag, the second pole $\arctan(f_c/f_2)$ = {{deg(atan(fT/(G*f2)))|°}}.
$\varphi_m \approx 90° - \arctan(f_c/f_2)$ = {{90 - deg(atan(fT/(G*f2)))|°}}. (The second pole also lowers $|AB|$ at $f_c$, by up to 3 dB when $f_c = f_2$, so the true crossover is a little lower and the margin a few degrees better, as the study card's slider shows.)

steps.prompt: Why is a unity-gain-stable op amp slower than a 'decompensated' version of the same design?
options: Its dominant pole is set so the loop is stable even with $B = 1$, which pushes $f_T$ (and the slew rate) down
It has a lower supply voltage
Its output stage has a higher output resistance
It uses FET inputs, which are slow
steps.explanation: With $B = 1$ the loop gain crosses 1 at $f_T$ itself, so $f_T$ must stay below the second pole. A decompensated op amp assumes a noise gain of, say, ≥ 5: crossover is then at $f_T/5$, so $f_T$ and the slew rate can be about 5× higher.

steps.prompt: The graph shows an op amp's open-loop gain. Read $f_T$ and estimate the bandwidth of a noninverting amplifier with gain {{G}}.
steps.explanation: The curve crosses 0 dB at $f_T$ ≈ {{A0*f0|Hz}} (it falls 20 dB per decade). The noise gain is {{G}} ({{20*log10(G)|dB}}), so $f_{-3dB} \approx f_T/G$ = {{A0*f0/G|Hz}}: where the open-loop curve drops to {{20*log10(G)|dB}}.

steps.prompt: A unity-gain follower ($f_T$ = {{fT|Hz}}, open-loop output resistance $R_o$ = {{Ro|Ω}}) drives a cable of $C_L$ = {{CL|F}}.

ask.prompt: At what frequency is the extra pole caused by the load?
ask.explanation: $R_o$ and $C_L$ form a low-pass inside the loop: $f_p = \frac{1}{2\pi R_oC_L}$ = 1/(2π × {{Ro|Ω}} × {{CL|F}}) = {{fp|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Estimate the phase margin that this pole leaves (crossover at $f_T$).
ask.explanation:
$f_p = 1/(2\pi R_oC_L)$ = {{fp|Hz}}. At the crossover $f_T$ it adds $\arctan(f_T/f_p)$ = {{deg(atan(fT/fp))|°}} of lag:
$\varphi_m \approx 90° -$ {{deg(atan(fT/fp))|°}} = {{90 - deg(atan(fT/fp))|°}} (ignoring the op amp's own second pole; the load pole also pulls the crossover down, so the true margin is somewhat larger). Much below 45° means ringing or oscillation; cure it with a 50–100 Ω series resistor outside the loop.

steps.prompt: A single-supply amplifier on {{Vcc|V}} has its output biased at $V_{CC}/2$. The op amp swings to within {{hr|V}} of each rail and delivers at most 20 mA.

ask.prompt: Find the largest undistorted peak output amplitude with no load.
ask.explanation: From $V_{CC}/2$ = {{Vcc/2|V}} the output can move {{Vcc/2|V}} − {{hr|V}} = {{Vcc/2 - hr|V}} up or down before it hits a limit.

ask.prompt: Now an ac-coupled load of {{RL|Ω}} is connected. Find the largest undistorted peak amplitude.
ask.explanation: Swing limit: $V_{CC}/2 - V_{headroom}$ = {{Vcc/2 - hr|V}}. Current limit: 20 mA × {{RL|Ω}} = {{0.02*RL|V}}. The smaller one wins: {{min(Vcc/2 - hr, 0.02*RL)|V}}.

lessons.title: Comparators, Schmitt triggers and real designs

steps.title: Positive feedback: the Schmitt trigger
steps.body: Feed part of the output back to the **+** input. When the output is high, the + input sits at an upper threshold; once $v_{in}$ crosses it, the output flips and the threshold jumps down. Noise smaller than the hysteresis can no longer cause multiple transitions. Use a real comparator for this when speed matters: an op amp without negative feedback slews slowly and recovers slowly from saturation.

steps.prompt: Inverting Schmitt trigger, output ±{{Vsat|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the upper threshold.
ask.explanation: With the output at +{{Vsat|V}} the divider sets $v_+ = V_{sat}\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}$ = {{Vsat|V}} × {{R1|Ω}}/{{R1+R2|Ω}} = {{Vsat*R1/(R1+R2)|V}}. When $v_{in}$ rises past this, the output swings low.

ask.prompt: Find the hysteresis (difference between the thresholds).
ask.explanation: The thresholds are $\pm V_{sat}\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}$ = ±{{Vsat*R1/(R1+R2)|V}}, so $\Delta V$ = {{2*Vsat*R1/(R1+R2)|V}}.

steps.prompt: Noninverting Schmitt trigger, output ±{{Vsat|V}}, − input grounded.

ask.prompt: The output is low. At what input voltage does it switch high?
ask.explanation: Superposition at the + input: $v_+ = \frac{v_{in}R_2 + v_oR_1}{R_1+R_2}$. It switches when $v_+$ crosses 0: $v_{in} = -v_o\frac{R_1}{R_2}$. With $v_o = -V_{sat}$: $v_{in}$ = {{Vsat|V}} × {{R1|Ω}}/{{R2|Ω}} = {{Vsat*R1/R2|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the hysteresis.
ask.explanation: The thresholds are $\pm V_{sat}R_1/R_2$ = ±{{Vsat*R1/R2|V}}, so $\Delta V = 2V_{sat}R_1/R_2$ = {{2*Vsat*R1/R2|V}}.

steps.prompt: Single-supply inverting Schmitt trigger: a comparator with push-pull output (0 V or {{Vcc|V}}), $R_A$ = {{Ra|Ω}}, $R_B$ = {{Rb|Ω}}, $R_F$ = {{Rf|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find the upper threshold (output high).
ask.explanation:
Output at $V_{CC}$: $R_F$ is in parallel with $R_A$ (both to $V_{CC}$), {{par(Ra,Rf)|Ω}}.
$V_H = V_{CC}\frac{R_B}{R_B + R_A\parallel R_F}$ = {{VH|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the lower threshold (output low).
ask.explanation:
Output at 0 V: $R_F$ is in parallel with $R_B$ (both to ground), {{par(Rb,Rf)|Ω}}.
$V_L = V_{CC}\frac{R_B\parallel R_F}{R_A + R_B\parallel R_F}$ = {{VL|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the hysteresis.
ask.explanation:
Output high: $V_H = V_{CC}R_B/(R_B + R_A\parallel R_F)$ = {{VH|V}}. Output low: $V_L = V_{CC}(R_B\parallel R_F)/(R_A + R_B\parallel R_F)$ = {{VL|V}}.
$\Delta V$ = {{VH-VL|V}}.

steps.prompt: Design an inverting Schmitt trigger (output ±{{Vsat|V}}) with {{dV|V}} hysteresis. With $R_1$ = 10 kΩ, what $R_2$ is needed?
steps.explanation: $\Delta V = 2V_{sat}\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}$ → $R_1 + R_2 = \frac{2V_{sat}R_1}{\Delta V}$ → $R_2 = R_1\left(\frac{2V_{sat}}{\Delta V} - 1\right)$ = 10 kΩ × ({{2*Vsat/dV}} − 1) = {{10000*(2*Vsat/dV - 1)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Why is a general-purpose op amp a poor comparator for a 100 kHz signal?
options: Its compensation limits the slew rate and it recovers slowly from saturation
Its input bias current is too high
Its open-loop gain is too low
It cannot be used without negative feedback at all
steps.explanation: An op amp is compensated for stability with feedback: slew rates of 0.5–15 V/µs mean several µs per transition, plus a delay to come out of saturation. A comparator has no compensation and switches in tens of ns. Using an op amp open loop is allowed, just slow.

steps.title: Diodes inside the loop
steps.body: Put a diode inside the feedback loop and the op amp hides its 0.6 V drop: the output follows the input with an error of only $V_F/A$. That gives a **precision rectifier**, and with a hold capacitor $C_H$ an **active peak detector**: $C_H$ charges to the highest input voltage. Follow it with a FET-input buffer; leakage then lets $C_H$ droop at $dV/dt = I_{leak}/C_H$. Speed is limited by the slew rate, as the op amp output must jump across the diode drop.

steps.prompt: A peak detector's hold capacitor $C_H$ = {{CH|F}} is discharged by a total leakage (diode, buffer input, capacitor) of {{Il|A}}.

ask.prompt: Find the droop rate in V/s.
ask.explanation: $\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{I_{leak}}{C_H}$ = {{Il|A}} / {{CH|F}} = {{Il/CH}} V/s.

ask.prompt: How long can it hold the peak before it has drooped by 10 mV?
ask.explanation: $t = \frac{C_H\Delta V}{I_{leak}}$ = {{CH|F}} × 10 mV / {{Il|A}} = {{0.01*CH/Il|s}}. A larger $C_H$ holds longer, but the op amp must charge it faster (output current limit).

steps.prompt: A noninverting amplifier with gain {{G}} uses an op amp with $f_T$ = {{fT|Hz}}, SR = {{SR/1e6}} V/µs and $V_{os}$ = {{Vos|V}}, on ±15 V supplies (output limit ±13 V).

ask.prompt: Find the small-signal bandwidth.
ask.explanation: $f_{-3dB} \approx f_T/G$ = {{fT|Hz}} / {{G}} = {{fT/G|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the largest undistorted peak output at 20 kHz.
ask.explanation: Slew limit: $\frac{SR}{2\pi f}$ = {{SR/1e6}} × 10⁶ V/s / (2π × 20 kHz) = {{SR/(2*pi*2e4)|V}}. Output limit: 13 V. The smaller one counts: {{min(SR/(2*pi*2e4), 13)|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the output offset with the input grounded.
ask.explanation: $V_{os}$ is amplified by the noise gain {{G}}: {{Vos|V}} × {{G}} = {{Vos*G|V}}.

steps.prompt: An inverting Schmitt trigger (output ±$V_{sat}$, thresholds $\pm V_{th}$) starts with $v_{in}$ far below zero. Put the events in order as $v_{in}$ rises slowly and then falls again.
items: Output at $+V_{sat}$; the + input sits at $+V_{th}$
Output flips to $-V_{sat}$; the + input drops to $-V_{th}$
Small dips in $v_{in}$ cause no new transition
$v_{in}$ falls below $-V_{th}$ and the output flips back high
steps.explanation: Positive feedback moves the threshold away from the input as soon as the output flips, so the input must travel the full hysteresis $2V_{th}$ before the next transition. That is what makes the output clean with a noisy, slowly varying input.
